title: The Board Risk Briefing
learningObjective: Communicate incident facts, uncertainty, business impact and decisions to leadership without overstating attribution or assurance.
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics explainer with narration, separate captions and no autoplay audio
visualStyle: Deep navy/charcoal with restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights, limited purple accents, high contrast, stable typography and reduced-motion transitions.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A board meeting is scheduled two hours after a suspected compromise of a customer-facing platform. The response team has isolated two hosts, but the scope of data access is still under investigation. The board chair asks for a definitive statement that no customer data was accessed and wants an exact recovery time.
scenes.direction: Use a fictional organization, synthetic people and generic systems. Do not expose real identity, secrets or operational infrastructure.

scenes.name: Decision frame
scenes.visual: Communicate incident facts, uncertainty, business impact and decisions to leadership without overstating attribution or assurance.
scenes.direction: Show the decision context and the relevant business/security trade-off. Avoid unsupported claims.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option C: Provide verified facts, known business impacts, containment already taken, current unknowns and confidence levels; explain next decision points, accountable owners, communication/legal review paths and a time for the next update rather than making unsupported assurances. Correct. Clear separation of verified facts, assumptions and unknowns supports governance decisions without overstating certainty.
scenes.direction: Animate a safe, high-level decision sequence; do not provide attack steps or sensitive operational detail.

scenes.name: Trade-offs
scenes.visual: Option A: No confirmed exfiltration does not prove that data was not accessed. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof. Option B: Leadership needs timely decision-ready information before attribution is complete. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof. Option D: Raw logs and attacker speculation can expose sensitive information and mislead leaders. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.
scenes.direction: Present the alternatives as decision cards and explain their risks without depicting an actual attack.

scenes.name: Takeaway
scenes.visual: Use a structured incident briefing: what happened, what is confirmed, what remains unknown, business impact, actions taken, decisions needed, owner and next update time. Coordinate external and regulatory communications with authorized stakeholders. Good incident governance makes uncertainty visible and assigns decisions; it does not conceal uncertainty or turn it into assurance.
scenes.direction: End with concise defensive action and keep text on screen long enough to read.

narration: Scenario: Two hosts are isolated after a suspected platform compromise, but data-access scope and recovery time remain unknown. Safest response: brief the board on verified facts, impacts, containment, uncertainties, owners and the next update. Option A is unsafe because No confirmed exfiltration does not prove that data was not accessed. Option B is unsafe because Leadership needs timely decision-ready information before attribution is complete. Option D is unsafe because Raw logs and attacker speculation can expose sensitive information and mislead leaders. In practice: separate facts, assumptions and unknowns, then record decisions and the update cadence. Key takeaway: communicate uncertainty clearly; do not promise what evidence cannot support.
audioDirection: Neutral, clear instructional narration; do not imitate a real person.
